paragraphs.heading: Points scattered by chance
paragraphs.text: A Poisson point process is a mathematical object made of points dropped at random onto a space. Its defining feature is that the points land independently of one another. Its name comes from a simple fact: count the points inside any finite region and that count has a Poisson distribution. Both the process and the distribution are named after the French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson.

paragraphs.heading: Two key properties
paragraphs.text: Every Poisson point process has two properties that matter wherever it is used. The first is the Poisson property: the count of points in any bounded region is a Poisson random variable. The second is independence: if you take regions that do not overlap, the count in each one tells you nothing about the counts in the others. This second property goes by names such as complete randomness or independent scattering. Because regions do not interact, the process is sometimes called purely or completely random.

paragraphs.heading: Rate and intensity
paragraphs.text: The process depends on a single quantity. When that quantity is a constant, it is called the rate or intensity, and it gives the average density of points in a region. That version is called a homogeneous or stationary Poisson point process. The constant λ can be read as the average number of points per unit of length, area, volume or time. If instead the average density changes from place to place, the process is called inhomogeneous or nonhomogeneous.

paragraphs.heading: Events along a line
paragraphs.text: On the real number line, the points can be treated as events, or arrivals. The number of events in any interval of length t is then a Poisson random variable with mean λt, so λ is the expected number of arrivals per unit of time. The gaps between events are called interarrival times, and they follow an exponential distribution with mean 1/λ. This gives the points a memoryless property: one point lying in an interval does not change the chances of others being there. That property has no natural match when the process lives in more dimensions.

paragraphs.heading: Where it shows up
paragraphs.text: The process was discovered more than once, independently, in work on radioactive decay, telephone call arrivals and actuarial science. In queueing theory it models random events spread over time, such as customers arriving at a store, calls reaching a telephone exchange, or earthquakes. Spread over a plane, it can describe where scattered things sit: transmitters in a wireless network, particles striking a detector, or trees in a forest. It serves as a model in fields from astronomy and ecology to economics and telecommunications.
